source.title: Rapid Convergence of the Unadjusted Langevin Algorithm: Isoperimetry Suffices

checks.paper_location: Section 2.2, equations (2) and (4), page 4
checks.claim: The functional inequality applies to density tests.
checks.note: The assumed LSI applies to strictly positive \(C^1\) relative densities of probability measures. At each positive time, Gaussian convolution produces such a density. Its Fisher information is finite, and LSI then implies finite relative entropy. The bounded exponential densities used to compare the LSI and Lipschitz constants also belong to this test class. No enlargement of the LSI test class is needed.

checks.paper_location: Section 3, equation (11); Appendix B.2.1, equations (28)-(29), pages 5 and 17
checks.claim: \(X_t=X_0-t\nabla U(X_0)+\sqrt{2t}\,Z\), with independent \(Z\sim\mathcal N(0,I)\).
checks.note: The transition is the image of the product of the current distribution and standard Gaussian measure under the displayed map. It equals the initial law at elapsed time zero and the next ULA law at elapsed time \(h\). The proof identifies its Gaussian mixture density, relative density and weak equation. The dimension is the real vector-space dimension; the zero-dimensional case is proved separately.

checks.paper_location: Appendix B.2.1, after equation (33), page 19
checks.claim: \(\mathbb E\lVert X_t-X_0\rVert^2=t^2\mathbb E\lVert\nabla U(X_0)\rVert^2+2tn\).
checks.note: Expanding the squared displacement gives a drift square, a Gaussian square and a mixed term. The mixed expectation is zero by independence and the zero Gaussian mean. The standard Gaussian second moment is \(n\). The assumptions require a finite squared-gradient moment, and do not require a second moment of the initial position. The identity also holds in dimension zero.

checks.paper_location: Appendix B.2.1, Gaussian interpolation preceding equation (30), pages 17-18
checks.claim: For every positive elapsed time, the Gaussian interpolation has a finite strictly positive mixture density and a normalized density relative to Gibbs measure.
checks.note: For positive time, each component Gaussian density is strictly positive and has a uniform finite upper bound. Their probability mixture is therefore finite and strictly positive, and Tonelli proves its normalization. Spatial differentiation under the initial probability integral proves \(C^1\) regularity. Averaging the component scores gives the mixture score and its Fisher estimate. Differentiation in time and integration by parts give the weak equation.

checks.paper_location: Appendix B.2.1, entropy calculation preceding equation (32), page 18
checks.claim: Density differentiation and integration by parts produce the entropy derivative.
checks.note: The argument first applies the fundamental theorem of calculus and Fubini to bounded smooth functions of the logarithmic density. The time derivative of the Gaussian kernel is integrable in space and time. Dominated convergence identifies the entropy values at the two times and the integrated flux as the logarithmic truncation is removed. The resulting entropy identity gives local absolute continuity and its derivative almost everywhere. Pointwise differentiability of the entropy at zero is not assumed.

checks.paper_location: Appendix B.2.1, equations (30)-(32), page 18
checks.claim: The frozen-drift equation determines entropy production.
checks.note: The Gaussian flux calculation proves the weak equation for bounded \(C^1\) tests whose gradients are square-integrable. Bounded logarithmic truncations satisfy these conditions. Their entropy identity converges by dominated convergence. Averaging the component Gaussian score then gives the mixture score in the derivative formula. Thus the final theorem does not assume validity of the weak equation for an arbitrary unbounded entropy test.

checks.paper_location: Appendix B.2.1, integrating-factor entropy comparison, pages 18-19
checks.claim: The affine scalar entropy comparison requires derivatives only in the open interval and continuity at the endpoints.
checks.note: On every compact positive-time interval, entropy is absolutely continuous and satisfies the differential inequality almost everywhere. An integrating factor gives the affine comparison on that interval. To pass the lower time to zero, the proof constructs a continuous function \(M\) with \(H(t)\le M(t)\) and \(M(0)=H(0)\). The separate comparison based on ordinary interior derivatives retains continuity at both endpoints as a hypothesis.

checks.paper_location: Appendix B.2.1, equation (33), page 18
checks.claim: Young's inequality leaves the Fisher coefficient \(-3/4\).
checks.note: The Gaussian entropy derivative is minus Fisher information plus the inner product of the gradient discrepancy with the relative score. The two factors are square-integrable. Cauchy–Schwarz and the nonnegative square \((\|a\|-\|b\|/2)^2\) give \(\langle a,b\rangle\le\|a\|^2+\|b\|^2/4\). Substituting this inequality leaves \(-3/4\) of Fisher information. The remaining discrepancy integral is bounded by the Gaussian displacement second moment.

checks.paper_location: Appendix B.2.1, equation (33) and its following displacement calculation, pages 18-19
checks.claim: The joint gradient-error energy is bounded by \(L^2\) times displacement energy.
checks.note: Gradient Lipschitzness gives a pointwise bound by \(L^2\) times the squared displacement. The displacement identity proves its integrability under the independent initial-state and Gaussian product measure. Integration gives \(L^2(t^2G_0+2tn)\). The numerical discrepancy bound is a conclusion of this argument.

checks.paper_location: Appendix B.2.1, equations (31)-(33), page 18
checks.claim: The entropy error pairing can be integrated under the joint law of \(X_0\) and \(X_t\).
checks.note: One proof represents the conditional expectation of the gradient discrepancy given the interpolated state by a measurable vector field. Conditional Jensen bounds its second moment, and the conditional-expectation identity transfers its integrals against observed tests. The final convergence proof instead computes the same pairing directly under the joint Gaussian law by averaging component scores. It therefore needs no choice of conditional field that is jointly measurable in time.

checks.paper_location: Appendix B.2.1, Lemma 9, page 16
checks.claim: \(\mathbb E_\nu\lVert\nabla U\rVert^2\le nL\).
checks.note: Translation invariance and the Lipschitz quadratic upper bound give a sub-Gaussian moment-generating-function estimate for the Gibbs score. Its directional second moments sum to nL, and the argument proves square-integrability. Strong convexity and a Hessian assumption are unnecessary when Gibbs normalization is given. A coupling-based comparison is available under an explicit coupling hypothesis; the final theorem obtains the current gradient moment directly from finite relative entropy.

checks.paper_location: Section 3.1, Lemma 3 and Theorem 2; end of Appendix B.2.1 and Appendix B.2.2, pages 6 and 19
checks.claim: The step restriction is \(0<h\le\alpha/(4L^2)\).
checks.note: In positive dimension, bounded exponential tests in LSI give a variance estimate for bounded \(C^1\) functions. Integration by parts with the Gibbs score and application to sine tests show \(\alpha\le L\). The final theorem handles dimension zero using uniqueness of probability measures on a singleton. The positive constants and the displayed step restriction remain assumptions; \(\alpha\le L\) is derived.

checks.paper_location: Section 3.1, Lemma 3, equation (12); Appendix B.2.1, final scalar calculation, pages 6 and 19
checks.claim: \(H(h)\le e^{-\alpha h}H(0)+6h^2nL^2\).
checks.note: The gradient moment bound gives a constant differential error \(b=(\alpha/4)H(0)+(5/2)hnL^2\). Apply affine comparison with \(a=3\alpha/2\) and use \((1-e^{-ah})/a\le h\). The inequality \(e^{-3x/2}+x/4\le e^{-x}\), for \(x=\alpha h\in[0,1/4]\), then gives the coefficient \(5/2\), which is enlarged to \(6\). The source proof instead bounds the differential error by \(3hnL^2\) and uses an exponential upper bound after applying an integrating factor. The final conclusion and step restriction agree.

checks.paper_location: Appendix B.2.2, first displayed bound, page 19
checks.claim: Iteration yields \(H_k\le e^{-\alpha hk}H_0+8hnL^2/\alpha\).
checks.note: Induction retains the geometric factor \(1-e^{-\alpha hk}\) in the accumulated error. The inequality \(1-e^{-x}\ge3x/4\) for \(0\le x\le1/4\) follows from the exponential tangent bound and a reciprocal estimate. With \(x=\alpha h\), substitution gives \(6h^2nL^2/(1-e^{-\alpha h})\le8hnL^2/\alpha\).

checks.paper_location: Section 3.1, Theorem 2, page 6
checks.claim: The convergence estimate concerns the distributions of the Gaussian ULA recursion.
checks.note: The final bound concerns ULA with independent standard Gaussian innovations. Its assumptions are differentiability, a Lipschitz gradient, LSI for the Gibbs target, positive constants, the step restriction and finite initial relative entropy. The proof establishes the Gaussian density, space and time regularity, weak equation, entropy differentiation, finite Fisher information and entropy, the estimate near zero, the gradient moment and \(\alpha\le L\). It then derives and iterates the entropy recurrence. Conditional interpolation variants retain their additional hypotheses.

checks.paper_location: Sections 2.1 and 3.1; Theorem 2 and Appendix B.2.2, pages 3, 6 and 19
checks.claim: The reference paper also gives an accuracy threshold and discusses Gaussian initialization.
checks.note: The initial measure is any probability measure with finite relative entropy. No initial Gaussian density, Fisher bound or position second moment is required. The proof establishes finite relative entropy at every iterate. A separate logarithmic iteration threshold for a prescribed error and a separate stationary-bias corollary are not stated as LSI theorems here.

checks.paper_location: Section 2.3.1, Theorem 1; Appendix B.1.3, pages 5 and 16
checks.claim: Continuous Langevin entropy decays at rate \(2\alpha\).
checks.note: The continuous comparison has factor \(e^{-2\alpha t}\), whereas the discrete theorem has factor \(e^{-\alpha hk}\). The continuous statement assumes a positive regular density path with finite energies and an entropy-dissipation identity. Under these assumptions, LSI implies the rate \(2\alpha\). This conditional result does not construct a Langevin stochastic differential equation or prove a transport inequality.

verdict: The ULA entropy bound is proved from differentiability, a globally Lipschitz gradient, LSI for the Gibbs target, positive constants, the stated step restriction and finite initial relative entropy. The proof establishes the density and all the analytic estimates used in the recurrence. The update, LSI convention, convergence rate and constants 6 and 8 agree with the 2019 theorem. The direct gradient-moment estimate, bounded-test proof of \(\alpha\le L\), bounded logarithmic chain rule and entropy estimate near zero are differences in the proof. Conditional interpolation results retain their additional assumptions. The discrete theorem does not include construction of a continuous Langevin process, a separate iteration threshold or a separate stationary-bias corollary.
